parole.significato: An indigenous Muscogee people of central Alabama.
parole.testo: Probably from French Alibamou or Alibamon, from Spanish Alibamo, from Alabama albaamo, the name for a member of a people native to the area.

parole.significato: A small recessed area set off from a larger room.
parole.testo: From French alcôve, from Spanish alcoba or Portuguese alcova, from Arabic القُبَّة (al-qubba, “vault, chamber with vaulted roof”). Doublet of qubba.

parole.significato: A type of sighting device used for measuring angles.
parole.testo: From French alidade, from Spanish alidada, from Arabic العِضَادَة (al-ʕiḍāda), perhaps from عَضُد (ʕaḍud, “upper arm”).

parole.significato: A herbaceous plant of the nightshade family (Alkekengi officinarum).
parole.testo: Through French alkékenge, Spanish alquequenje, from Arabic كَاكَنْج (kākanj).

parole.significato: White barley sugar
parole.testo: From French alphénic, alfénic, from Spanish alfeñique, from Arabic فَانِيد (fānīd), from Persian پانید (pânid, “sugar candy”).

parole.significato: Synonym of beekeeper.
parole.testo: From French apiculteur and Spanish apicultor.

parole.significato: Any member of the species Crataegus azarolus of shrubs of southern Europe, related to hawthorn.
parole.testo: From French azerole, from Spanish acerola, from Andalusian Arabic الزَعْرُورَة (az-zaʕrúra), from Classical Arabic زُعْرُورَة (zuʕrūra). Doublet of acerola.

parole.significato: An Asiatic tree (Melia azedarach), common in the southern United States, commonly called bead tree, chinaberry, etc.
parole.testo: From French azédarach, from Spanish acederaque, from Arabic أَزَادَرْخَت (ʔazādarḵat), from Persian آزاددرخت (âzâd-deraxt), from آزاد (âzâd, “noble”) + درخت (deraxt, “tree”).

parole.significato: The residue from processing sugar cane or other plants such as sorghum or sugar beet after the juice is extracted.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French bagasse, from Spanish bagazo (“plant residue (especially from sugar cane) after juice is extracted”), from baga (“berry”) (from Latin bāca (“berry or other small fruit; etc.”); further etymology uncertain) + -azo (augmentative suffix).

parole.significato: A barricade.
parole.testo: The noun is from French barricade, from barrique (“cask”) + -ade (“group”); or Spanish barricada, from barrica (“cask”) + -ada (“group”). So named after the first street barricades in Paris, which were composed of casks filled with earth, paving stones, etc. The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: To solicit money by entertaining the public in the street or in public transport.
parole.testo: Apparently from French busquer or Spanish buscar.

parole.significato: A tree (known as the calabash tree; Crescentia cujete) native to Central and South America, the West Indies, and southe…
parole.testo: From French calebasse, from Spanish calabaza (“gourd; pumpkin”), possibly from Arabic قَرْعَةٌ يَابِسَةٌ (qarʕatun yābisatun, “dry gourd”) or directly from its etymon Persian خربزه (xarboze, “melon”), possibly ultimately from Sanskrit त्रपुस (trapusa, “colocynth fruit”) (compare Persian تربزه (tarbo

parole.significato: The edible greenish material found underneath the upper half of a turtle's carapace (shell).
parole.testo: From French carapace, Spanish carapacho; further etymology uncertain. Doublet of carapace.

parole.significato: A small, usually yellow, finch (genus Serinus), a songbird native to the Canary Islands.
parole.testo: From French canarie, from Spanish canario, from the Latin Canariae insulae (“Canary Islands”) (Spanish Islas Canarias); from the largest island Insula Canaria (“Dog Island" or "Canine Island”), named for its dogs, from canārius (“canine”), from canis (“dog”).

parole.significato: Latex; natural rubber.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French caoutchouc, from Spanish caucho, from Quechua kawchu. Doublet of caucho.

parole.significato: A hard protective covering of bone or chitin, especially one which covers the dorsal portion of an animal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French carapace (“tortoise shell”), from Spanish carapacho, of unknown origin, but likely from an extinct Ibero-Mediterranean substrate language. Compare Catalan carabassa, Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”), Latin scarabaeus (the source of scarab); also Spanish galápago (“kind

parole.significato: A cargo; a load of goods transported.
parole.testo: From French cargaison, Spanish cargazón, from Latin cargare (“to load”). See cargo.

parole.significato: A shot in which the ball struck with the cue comes in contact with two or more balls on the table; a hitting of two or…
parole.testo: Probably derived from French carambole (the red ball in billiards).

parole.significato: A box or vase with a perforated cover to emit perfumes.
parole.testo: From French cassolette, from Spanish cazoleta (“pan”).

parole.significato: A person who resolves cases of conscience or moral duty.
parole.testo: From French casuiste, from Spanish casuista, from Latin casus (“case”).

parole.significato: A slow, stately Baroque dance.
parole.testo: From French chaconne, from Spanish chacona, likely from Basque txukun (“pretty”).

parole.significato: A descendant of European settlers who is born in a colonized country.
parole.testo: Variously from French créole, from its source, Spanish criollo, and from its source, Portuguese crioulo, itself probably a diminutive of cria (“person raised in one’s house, servant”), from criar (“to rear, to bring up”), from Latin creō (“to create, make, produce”). Doublet of Criollo, Crioulo, and

parole.significato: sea bream
parole.testo: Borrowed from French daurade, itself borrowed, through the intermediate of an Italian text, from Spanish dorada, partially from Latin aurāta, and influenced by the verb dorar (“gild, give a golden color”). Doublet of dorado.

parole.significato: A pier, a wharf.
parole.testo: From French embarcadère, from Spanish embarcadero.

parole.significato: To disrupt someone's composure or comfort with acting publicly or freely.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French embarrasser, from Middle French embarrasser, embarasser (“to embarrass; to block, obstruct”), from Spanish embarazar, either from Italian imbarazzare or from Portuguese embaraçar.

parole.significato: common sainfoin (Onobrychis sativa)
parole.testo: From French esparcet, esparcette, éparcet, from Spanish esparceta, esparcilla.

parole.significato: A dais or raised platform.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French estrade, from Spanish estrado. Doublet of stratum and street.

parole.significato: Synonym of Kari'na (“An indigenous people native to the north coast of South America”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Galibi, ultimately from Spanish Caribe via an indigenous intermediate, possibly Karipúna Creole French or another creole. Doublet of Carib; further related to cannibal, caribe, Carijona, Garifuna, and Kari'na.

parole.significato: Huge; immense; tremendous.
parole.testo: From French Gargantua, a giant with a very large appetite in Rabelais's The Inestimable Life of Gargantua. Rabelais derived Gargantua from the Portuguese and Spanish garganta (“throat”).

parole.significato: A species of parrot (Bolbopsittacus lunulatus) endemic to the Philippines.
parole.testo: From French guaiabero, from Spanish guayaba.

parole.significato: The administrator of an opera house or theater.
parole.testo: Originally and usually from French intendant, but translating Spanish or Chinese equivalents in some contexts.

parole.significato: Unwillingness to change one's views or to agree.
parole.testo: From French intransigeance, noun form of intransigeant, borrowed from Spanish intransigente at the end of the nineteenth century. Morphologically, from in- + transiger + -ant, literally "uncompromising".

parole.significato: Unwilling to compromise or moderate a position; unreasonable; stubborn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intransigeant, from Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- (“un-, not”) + trānsigēns, present participle of trānsigō (“to come to an understanding”), from trāns (“across”) + agō (“to do”).

parole.significato: A semiprecious stone, either nephrite or jadeite, generally green or white in color, often used for carving figurines.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French le jade, rebracketing of earlier l'éjade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), via Vulgar Latin *iliata from Latin ilia (“flank”). (Jade was thought to cure pains in the side.)

parole.significato: A fragrant bulb flower (Narcissus jonquilla), a species of daffodil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jonquille, itself a borrowing from Spanish junquillo. Possible doublet of junket.

parole.significato: Any of several green citrus fruit, somewhat smaller and sharper-tasting than a lemon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lime, from Spanish lima, from Arabic لِيمَة (līma), from Classical Persian لِیمُو (līmū, līmō), from Sanskrit निम्बू (nimbū, “lime”), ultimately from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *limaw or Munda. Doublet of lemon.

parole.significato: Representing or personifying death.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French macabre, whose etymology is uncertain. Possibly from the term danse macabre, most commonly believed to be from corruption of the biblical name Maccabees; compare Latin Chorea Machabaeorum. Another theory derives the French term (through Spanish macabro) from Arabic مَقَابِر (maq

parole.significato: The second-highest trump in certain card games.
parole.testo: From French manille, influenced by Spanish manilla.

parole.significato: An escaped black slave of the Caribbean and the Americas or a descendant of such a person.
parole.testo: From French marron (“feral; fugitive”, adjective), from Spanish cimarrón (“fugitive, wild, feral”); see that entry for more.

parole.significato: A dressing made from vegetable oil, raw egg yolks, vinegar or lemon juice, and seasoning, used on salads, with French f…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French mayonnaise, possibly named after the city of Maó (Mahón in Spanish), Minorca, whence the recipe was brought back to France. Compare Spanish mahonesa. Alternative suggested origins include the city of Bayonne (bayonnaise); the Duke of Mayenne and the words manier (“to

parole.significato: A drink produced by adding alcohol to grape juice.
parole.testo: From French mistelle, Spanish mistela, from Italian mistella, from misto (“mixed”).

parole.significato: Of or characterized by an avoidance of laws against usury by a pair of sales between a lender and a borrower (or their…
parole.testo: From French, Spanish, or Latin mohatra, all from Arabic مُخَاطَرَة (muḵāṭara)

parole.significato: A shade of bright red-orange.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nacarat, from Spanish or Portuguese nacarado, ultimately derived from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra, “small drum”), from نَقَرَ (naqara, “to hollow out”). Related to English nacre, English naqareh and nagada.

parole.significato: rhea (large, flightless birds)
parole.testo: From French nandou from Spanish ñandú from Paraguayan Guarani ñandu guasu.

parole.significato: A crystalline mixture of hydrous sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, with the chemical formula Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
parole.testo: From French natron, from Spanish natrón, from Arabic نَطْرُون (naṭrūn), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron, “nitre”), ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj (“natron”): R9 Doublet of niter and trona.

parole.significato: A plantation of nopal (a prickly pear cactus of the genus Opuntia, especially Opuntia cochinellifera) used as food for…
parole.testo: From nopal + -ery (suffix forming nouns indicating places of arts, crafts, or practices), modelled after French nopalerie. Nopal is borrowed from Spanish nopal, from Classical Nahuatl nohpalli (“cactus of the genus Opuntia”), from Proto-Uto-Aztecan [Term?].

parole.significato: A Spanish card game, usually played by three people. It involves forty cards, omitting the ranks of 8, 9 and 10.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hombre, from Spanish hombre, literally, a man, from Latin homō. Doublet of gome, hombre, homo, and omi. See human.

parole.significato: A canoe of shallow draft, made by hollowing a log.
parole.testo: From French pirogue, in turn from Spanish piragua, from Kari'na piraua. Doublet of periagua.

parole.significato: A mixture of dried fragrant plant material, often in a decorative bowl, used to scent a room.
parole.testo: From French pot-pourri (“stew, potpourri”), a calque of Spanish olla podrida (“stew”, literally “rotten pot”). Doublet of olla podrida.

parole.significato: A point in the game of faro.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pointe or Spanish punto (“point”). Doublet of point, pointe, ponto, puncto, punctum, and punto.

parole.significato: A dance originating in the mid-1700s with four couples forming a square, rather much like the modern square dance.
parole.testo: French, in sense of “group of knights”, from Spanish cuadrilla, diminutive of cuadra (“square”) (compare also cuadra (“four”)), from Latin quadra.

parole.significato: A First Nations residential area within an Indian reserve in British Columbia.
parole.testo: From French rancherie, from Spanish ranchería. Doublet of rancheria.

parole.significato: A social upstart, especially from a Mediterranean or Latin American country; a smooth untrustworthy foreigner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rastaquouère, from South American Spanish rastacuero.

parole.significato: An outer garment typical of the Andes region of Venezuela and Colombia, and resembling a poncho.
parole.testo: From French ruana and its etymon, Spanish ruana (“woolen fabric or garment”), of disputed origin. Suggestions include Latin rūga (“wrinkle”), Quechua ruana (“textile”), and Chibcha ruana (“land of blankets”); see Wikipedia.

parole.significato: A Muslim holy man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French santon, from Spanish santón.

parole.significato: A 16th-century Spanish dance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sarabande, from Spanish zarabanda.

parole.significato: Fermented green forage fodder stored in an airtight silo or clamp.
parole.testo: Alteration (probably by influence of silo) of ensilage (1881), itself from French ensilage, from ensiler (“put in a silo”), from Spanish ensilar.

parole.significato: To avoid one's lessons or work (chiefly at school or university); shirk.
parole.testo: Probably from French esquiver (“slink away”), from Middle French esquiver (“to escape”), from Spanish esquivar (“to avoid, reject, elude”), from esquivo (“contemptuous, loathsome”), itself from Old French eschiver, of East Germanic origin, from Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌷𐍃 (*skiuhs, “afraid, barefaced”), from Pro

parole.significato: The ace of spades in ombre and quadrille.
parole.testo: From French spadille, from Spanish espadilla, diminutive of espada. Doublet of spathilla.

parole.significato: Articles made from esparto.
parole.testo: French sparterie, from Spanish esparto (“esparto”), Latin spartum from Ancient Greek σπάρτον (spárton, “rope, cable”).

parole.significato: Any of a few species of maize-like grasses of the genus Zea found in Mexico, Guatemala and Nicaragua.
parole.testo: From French téosinte, from Spanish teocinte, from Classical Nahuatl teocintli, apparently from teōtl (“god”) + cintli (“dried maize”).

parole.significato: A small two-masted, and later three-masted, Mediterranean transport ship with an overhanging bow and stern.
parole.testo: From French chebec, from Spanish xabeque or Catalan xabec or Italian sciabecco, from Arabic شُبَّاك (šubbāk, “fishing-net”). Not to confuse with the sambuq, an Indian-Sea vessel.

parole.significato: Ictonyx striatus, a small, carnivorous, nocturnal African mammal resembling a skunk.
parole.testo: From French zorille, from Spanish zorrillo, from zorro (“fox”) + -illo.
